title: Private Credit Defaults Hit Five-Year Highs as Shadow Loan Risks Mount
excerpt: Loan defaults at major private credit firms have reached their highest levels since at least 2021 while fund managers clamp down on payment-in-kind sweeteners amid growing fears of hidden losses.
body:
• Loan defaults at funds managed by Ares, Blackstone, Blue Owl Capital, and Golub Capital have hit their highest levels since at least 2021, with Blue Owl's default rate reaching 2.8% in Q2 2026.
  • Private-credit firms are pulling back on payment-in-kind (PIK) loan provisions — down from 25% of new loans to 13.5% in Q2 — amid concerns that deferred interest payments mask true default levels.
  • Fund returns have deteriorated from 10%-plus annual returns to below 7%, with one KKR-managed fund losing 6.55% over the past year, raising the prospect of a wave of retail investor redemptions.
  • Brookfield CEO Bruce Flatt and other industry leaders insist the stress is not systemic, while Golub Capital's co-CEO acknowledges the market is "clearly in a credit cycle."

Defaults Rise Across Major Funds

The $3 trillion private credit market is showing deepening fractures, with defaults climbing at funds run by some of the industry's biggest names even as their executives maintain that performance remains sound.

An analysis by The Wall Street Journal found that nonperforming loans at publicly traded funds overseen by Ares Management, Blackstone, Blue Owl Capital, and Golub Capital have all hit five-year highs, surpassing levels seen during the Federal Reserve's aggressive rate-hiking campaign in 2023. Blue Owl's fund reported a 2.8% default rate in the second quarter — its worst reading in at least five years.

"Some in the press have been saying 'Oh no, the sky is falling,' and some of my peers at other firms have been saying 'That's nonsense, there's no problem.' Neither of those is accurate. We are clearly in a credit cycle."

— David Golub, Co-Chief Executive, Golub Capital

The bad loans are concentrated so far in healthcare companies like dental-service provider Affordable Care and businesses affected by higher oil prices, including plastic-film manufacturer Loparex. The bigger worry for analysts: software companies, which make up 20% or more of many funds' portfolios and face potential disruption from artificial intelligence.

Shadow Default Fears Trigger PIK Clampdown

The stress has prompted lenders to tighten a once-popular deal sweetener that critics say has been masking the true scale of loan distress.

Payment-in-kind provisions — which let borrowers defer cash interest payments by adding the owed amount to their loan principal — dropped to just 13.5% of new private-credit loans originated in the second quarter, down sharply from 25% at the end of 2025, according to investment-banking adviser Lincoln International.

The provision came under scrutiny after software firm Medallia used PIK arrangements to defer interest payments for roughly four years before its $2.8 billion debt pile collapsed, rattling the industry. Now, private-credit executives increasingly view PIK as a warning sign that a loan may be souring.

"This is an evolution we are seeing unfolding now. The pendulum is shifting."

— Brian Garfield, Managing Director, Lincoln International

A separate analysis by Morningstar DBRS found that distressed exchange transactions — restructurings where borrowers defer all cash interest until maturity — accounted for 94% of downgrades to default or selective default status over the 12 months ending February 2026. MSCI, meanwhile, reported that 20%-plus writedowns on senior private-credit loans have more than tripled since 2022.

Returns Slide, Redemption Risks Grow

The performance deterioration extends beyond defaults. Funds that once routinely delivered 10%-plus annual returns are now struggling to clear 7%. A fund managed by KKR lost 6.55% over the 12 months through June 2026, only a marginal improvement from a 9.17% loss in the prior period.

Multiple forces are squeezing margins: a slowdown in private-equity dealmaking has curtailed the supply of lucrative new loans, weaker borrower performance has forced mark-to-market writedowns, and benchmark interest rate declines have trimmed the income funds earn on floating-rate loans.

Fund managers characterize the fluctuations as normal for a market focused on lower-rated corporate borrowers. But many individual investors who piled into private credit during the boom years have never experienced a downturn — and if returns stay flat or decline further, redemption requests could accelerate.

Industry Leaders Push Back

Despite the data, some of the industry's most prominent voices maintain that the market's fundamentals remain intact.

Blue Owl co-CEO Marc Lipschultz told analysts that "across our direct lending strategy, credit health remains strong" and that the firm's watchlist had seen "no meaningful change" from a year ago — a claim that makes Blue Owl an outlier, as watchlists at Ares, Golub, and KKR have all expanded to their highest levels since 2022–23.

Brookfield CEO Bruce Flatt has been among the most vocal defenders, writing in his shareholder letter that private credit is "simply credit" at its core and that the company's disciplined underwriting, focused on real-asset-backed lending, gives it "no material exposure to software." He has argued the stress is "definitely not" comparable to the 2008 financial crisis.

What to Watch

The immediate question is whether defaults remain contained in healthcare and energy or spread to the software sector that underpins much of the market. Ares Capital hired a consultant to review its software portfolio and found 85% of holdings face low AI disruption risk, but the remaining 15% — roughly 3.3% of total assets — remains vulnerable.

If interest rates decline and economic growth holds, losses could moderate. But fewer investors would mean less capital available to refinance corporate loans when they mature, potentially creating a feedback loop of tightening credit and rising defaults that tests even the most disciplined lenders.
